resources.string: Pawse uses this to know which app is on screen, so that it can cover the apps you chose to block. It reads which app owns each window and nothing inside it.
The session has been on for %1$s.
Boop your tag to end the session.
Since %1$s. Scan your tag to end the session.
Scan your tag to start a session.
The watcher is off. Pawse needs its accessibility service to know which app is on screen.
The watcher is switched on but not running, so nothing is being blocked. Switch Pawse off and on again in accessibility settings.
If Android says the setting is restricted: open Pawse’s app info, tap the three dots at the top, and choose “Allow restricted settings”. Then try again.
The phone may stop Pawse to save battery, and blocking would stop with it. On the page that opens, choose “No restrictions” or “Allow”.
NFC is switched off, so a tag cannot be read.
No key is registered. A key is an NFC tag that starts and ends a session.
No apps are on the block list.
This tag is not a key. The session is still on.
The block list cannot be changed during a session.
A key is an NFC tag. Scanning any of them starts a session, and scanning any of them ends it. To register a tag that already is a Pawse tag, hold it against the phone now.
Keys cannot be changed during a session.
This phone has no NFC, so it cannot use keys.
Hold a tag against the back of the phone and keep it there. Whatever is on the tag will be replaced.
This tag will be able to start and end sessions.
The tag will no longer start or end sessions. It can be registered again later.
This tag is already a key: %1$s.
This is not a Pawse tag. Use “Write a new key” to make it one.
This tag is too small: it holds %1$d bytes and a key needs %2$d.
This kind of tag cannot hold a key.
Writing failed. Hold the tag still against the phone and try again.
